evidence_quote: The moving assembly line system, which started on October 7, 1913, allowed Ford to reduce the price of his cars.
prompt: A carmaker builds one low-priced, standardized car that is in high demand; teams of workers assemble each car at fixed stations while parts are carried to them. Proposal (1913): rebuild the main plant so the car moves past stationary workers on a powered line, each worker doing one small repeated task, and pass the savings on to buyers as lower prices. Risks raised: the conversion is costly and disrupts output while it happens; repetitive work may drive high worker turnover; the line only pays off at very high volume of a single model; rivals offer more variety and buyers may tire of one design.

evidence_quote: It was the best-selling commercial aircraft until being surpassed by the competing Airbus A320 family in October 2019
prompt: A large airliner maker has no small jet for short routes; two rivals already sell small twin-jets and are a year or more ahead in airline orders. Proposal (1965): launch a small twin-engine short-haul jet that reuses the cabin cross-section of the company's larger jets, giving six-abreast seating that is wider than the rivals' five-abreast cabins, with the engines mounted under the wings. Risks raised: the company is late to the segment; launch orders are few; its engineering staff is stretched by other large programmes; the rivals may lock in the major airlines first.

evidence_quote: The Airbus A320 family is a series of narrow-body airliners developed and produced by Airbus, and is the best-selling airliner ever built.
prompt: A European aircraft consortium sells only wide-body jets; the 150-seat narrow-body market is held by an American maker's long-running model and a stretched rival design. Proposal (1984): launch a new 150-seat narrow-body with digital fly-by-wire controls, side-stick controllers and a cockpit shared with its future models, backed by government launch aid. Risks raised: fly-by-wire has never been used on a civil airliner and pilots and regulators may resist it; the incumbent can cut prices; launch orders come from only a few airlines; development costs are large for a consortium that is not yet profitable.

evidence_quote: Since its launch in 1987, more than 100 billion cans of Red Bull have been sold worldwide, including over 13.9 billion in 2025.
prompt: A toothpaste marketer has licensed a sweet caffeinated tonic that is sold in Asia mainly to manual workers and truck drivers. Proposal (1987): adapt it into a carbonated drink in a small slim can, launch it in its home country at a price well above colas, and market it to students, clubbers and extreme-sports fans as a new 'energy drink' category. Risks raised: consumers may dislike the taste; no such drink category exists in the region; the price is high for a small can; regulators in some countries may restrict its caffeine and taurine content.

evidence_quote: In June 1992, at the time of its initial public offering, Starbucks (ticker symbol: SBUX) had 140 outlets, with revenue of US$73.5 million, up from US$1.3 million in 1987.
prompt: A former marketing director runs a few small Italian-style espresso bars. The small local coffee-bean roaster and retailer he once worked for, with six stores, is for sale. Proposal (1987): buy the roaster, rename the espresso bars under its brand, and expand the combined chain of cafes selling espresso drinks to other cities. Risks raised: most of the country drinks cheap drip coffee and espresso drinks are a niche; the drinks cost several times the price of diner coffee; opening stores in distant cities needs heavy capital; the buyer must raise the purchase money from investors.

evidence_quote: The iMac G3 was an immediate hit with consumers, with 278,000 units sold in the first six weeks, and 800,000 units after 20 weeks.
prompt: A personal computer maker has lost money for two years and its market share is shrinking. Proposal (1998): launch a low-priced all-in-one consumer computer in a translucent colored case, with no diskette drive and none of the older ports, relying on a CD-ROM drive, the new USB standard and the internet for software and peripherals. Risks raised: buyers and reviewers expect a diskette drive; few USB peripherals exist yet; users' existing printers and drives will not connect; the company's finances leave little room for a miss.

evidence_quote: The PlayStation 2 remains the best-selling video game console of all time, having sold 160 million units worldwide
prompt: A console maker leads the home video-game market with its first console. Proposal (1999): make the next console play DVD movies as well as games, keep it backward-compatible with the previous console's games, and price it near rival consoles even though the DVD drive and new chips raise its cost. Risks raised: the hardware will sell at a loss at launch; chip yields may limit supply at launch; a rival console goes on sale a year earlier; developers find the new architecture hard to program.

evidence_quote: The feed is the primary system through which users are exposed to content posted on the network.
prompt: A fast-growing social network for students has just added a home page that streams a constantly updated list of friends' activity (profile changes, new photos, relationship updates) to every member. Many members complain that it is intrusive and violates their privacy, and protest groups against it are growing quickly. Proposal (2006): keep the feed, apologize, and add privacy controls that let members choose what appears in it. Risks raised: the complaints may turn into members leaving; nothing new is shared, it is only made more visible; the press coverage is negative; rivals may use the backlash to win members.

evidence_quote: With a market share of 71.22% across all platforms combined as of December 2025, Chrome is the most used web browser in the world.
prompt: A web search company's revenue depends on people using the web. One operating-system vendor's browser holds most of the market, and an open-source browser that the search company funds through a search deal holds most of the rest. Proposal (2008): build and release its own free browser, with a new fast JavaScript engine and each tab in a separate process, and open-source the code. Risks raised: the dominant browser comes preinstalled on most PCs; it may strain the relationship with the open-source browser it funds; the company has never shipped desktop software of this scale; users rarely switch browsers.

evidence_quote: As of March 2026, it is one of the largest providers of music streaming services, with over 777 million monthly active users comprising 300 million paying subscribers.
prompt: A startup has built a desktop app that streams almost any song instantly. Music piracy is widespread and record labels' sales are falling. Proposal (2008): launch in several European countries with a free tier funded by ads and a paid ad-free tier, after licensing the major labels' catalogs in exchange for upfront payments and equity. Risks raised: labels demand large minimum payments; ad revenue per listener is low; most users may never pay; free piracy remains easy.

evidence_quote: In total, Apple sold more than 15 million first-generation iPads prior to the launch of the iPad 2
prompt: A consumer-electronics company sells a very popular touchscreen phone with an app store. Tablet computers from several makers over the past decade sold poorly. Proposal (2010): launch a 10-inch tablet running the phone's operating system and apps, priced from $499, positioned between a phone and a laptop. Risks raised: critics call it just a big phone; it has no camera and cannot run several apps at once; earlier tablets found no mass market; small cheap laptops already sell for less.

evidence_quote: On December 1, 2020, Slack and Salesforce announced an agreement for Salesforce to acquire the company for approximately $27.7 billion.
prompt: A small game studio's online game has not found enough players to be profitable, and most of its venture money is left. The team built an internal chat tool with searchable history and integrations to coordinate its own work. Proposal (2013): close the game, lay off most staff, and turn the internal tool into a commercial team-messaging product for businesses. Risks raised: enterprise chat and email tools already exist; the team has no business-software experience; layoffs may hurt morale; investors backed a game, not a business tool.

evidence_quote: despite complaints, most of its 1.4 million subscribers planned to renew
prompt: A creative-software maker sells its design suite as a perpetual license costing thousands of dollars, with a new version every year or two; it also offers an optional monthly subscription. Proposal (2013): stop selling perpetual licenses and offer the suite only as a monthly subscription with continuous updates. Risks raised: many customers object loudly to renting their tools; customers lose access to the software if they stop paying; revenue will dip during the transition; some users may switch to cheaper rivals or pirated copies.

evidence_quote: The Golf is Volkswagen's bestseller and the third best-selling automobile of all time, with over 37 million units sold worldwide.
prompt: A carmaker's sales rest on a single long-running rear-engined, air-cooled small car whose sales are falling, and its other recent models have not caught on. Proposal (1974): replace it with a new front-engined, front-wheel-drive, water-cooled hatchback styled by an outside designer, built on new tooling during an oil crisis. Risks raised: loyal buyers love the old car's character; retooling is very expensive while profits are shrinking; the company has little experience with water-cooled front-drive cars; the oil crisis is shrinking car demand.

evidence_quote: it became one of the most popular and profitable mobile apps of 2016, amassing over 500 million downloads worldwide.
prompt: A small studio spun out of a large tech company runs a location-based mobile game with a modest, devoted player base and a map of real-world points of interest built by those players. Proposal (2016): partner with a famous creature-collecting game franchise to launch a free-to-play phone game in which players walk to real places to catch and battle creatures, earning money from in-app purchases. Risks raised: the studio's servers have only handled a small audience; walking around while staring at a phone raises safety concerns; free-to-play revenue depends on a small share of paying players; location games have stayed niche.

evidence_quote: The 32X is considered a commercial failure.
prompt: A console maker's 16-bit console is aging, and its next-generation 32-bit console is due in about a year. Proposal (1994): release an add-on that plugs into the 16-bit console to give it 32-bit graphics, priced at about $160, with games rushed to be ready for the holiday season, while the next-generation console proceeds on schedule. Risks raised: the add-on and the new console will compete for the same buyers and developers; the launch library will be small; the schedule is very tight; buyers may wait for the new console.

evidence_quote: The commercial failure of the Jaguar prompted Atari to leave the console market and restructure itself as a third-party developer.
prompt: A computer and game maker that was once a market leader has shrunk sharply and is winding down its home computers. Proposal (1993): launch a cartridge home console marketed as the first 64-bit system, priced at $249, with an initial release in two US cities and a handful of launch games, ahead of rival next-generation consoles. Risks raised: third-party developers have committed few games; the hardware is hard to program; the company has little cash for marketing; two large rivals will launch new consoles within a year.

evidence_quote: Dreamcast sales did not meet Sega's expectations, and attempts to renew interest through price cuts caused significant financial losses.
prompt: A console maker's previous console lost heavily and damaged its relations with retailers and developers, and the company is in financial trouble. The market leader's next console is expected in about a year. Proposal (1998): launch a new console with a built-in modem for online play, priced at $199, a year before the leader's next machine. Risks raised: the leader's announced next console may make buyers wait; several big third-party publishers are not committing games; the company's finances leave little room for selling hardware at a loss; its disc format may be easy to pirate.

evidence_quote: In April 2009, the company announced that it would end the United States GeoCities service on October 26, 2009.
prompt: A leading web portal wants more users and page views. Proposal (1999): buy a free personal-web-page hosting service, the third-most-visited site on the web, for about $3.6 billion in stock, and sell advertising across its millions of user pages. Risks raised: the hosting service's revenue is small for the price; advertisers dislike placing ads next to amateur content; new terms of service may anger the page owners; the price reflects a stock market at record highs.

evidence_quote: less than 2% of Terra's initial multibillion-dollar investment
prompt: A Spanish-language internet provider controlled by a large telecom company wants a big US presence. Proposal (2000): buy a major US web portal and search engine for about $12.5 billion in stock and combine the two into one global portal. Risks raised: the portal ranks behind larger rivals in traffic; the price is a large multiple of its revenue; integrating companies on two continents is hard; the combined company's stock price is volatile.

evidence_quote: The A380's estimated $25 billion development cost was not recouped by the time Airbus ended production.
prompt: An aircraft maker competes with a rival that has held the largest-airliner market for 30 years. Airlines are flying more routes point to point with smaller twin-engine jets, while major hub airports are congested. Proposal (2000): launch a double-deck airliner seating about 550, larger than any existing jet, with a development budget of about $10.7 billion and 50 firm orders from six launch customers. Risks raised: airports must modify gates and taxiways; the market for very large aircraft may be small; the rival may stretch its jumbo instead; development budgets may overrun.

evidence_quote: In the late 2000s, olestra lost popularity due to supposed side effects and is largely phased out
prompt: A consumer-goods company spent decades developing a fat substitute that passes through the body undigested. Regulators have approved it for savory snacks, with a required label statement about possible effects on the digestive system. Proposal (1998): launch a national line of fat-free potato chips made with it, under a new brand, with heavy advertising. Risks raised: the required label statement may scare buyers; consumer groups oppose the ingredient; the chips cost more than regular chips; dieters' attention may shift from fat to other concerns.

evidence_quote: In March 2000, BMW announced it planned to sell the Rover Group.
prompt: A premium German carmaker wants to broaden its range into small cars and four-wheel-drive vehicles. Proposal (1994): buy a loss-making British volume carmaker, including its respected off-road brand, from its aerospace parent for about £800 million, and invest heavily in new models. Risks raised: the British carmaker has lost money for years; its Japanese partner, which supplies much of its engineering, objects to the sale and may withdraw; the two companies' brands overlap in some segments; the British plants have low productivity.

evidence_quote: one of the worst deals ever made in the dotcom era
prompt: A web portal with a large ad business wants to reach young users through social networking. Proposal (2008): buy a social network popular with teenagers in the UK and Ireland for $850 million in cash and integrate it with the portal's instant-messaging service. Risks raised: a larger rival social network is growing fast in the same markets; the network's revenue is small relative to the price; the portal's own strategy has changed several times; social networks can lose users quickly.

evidence_quote: On August 4, 2010, Google announced Wave would no longer be developed as a stand-alone product due to a lack of interest.
prompt: A large web company has built a new communication tool that merges email, instant messaging and document editing into shared real-time conversations that anyone in them can edit and replay. Proposal (2009): open it by invitation to 100,000 users as a preview, then expand it as a replacement for email. Risks raised: early users find the interface confusing and are unsure what it is for; it is useful only if one's contacts also use it, and invitations are scarce; it runs slowly in current browsers; it does not interoperate with existing email.

evidence_quote: It was a commercial failure; with 13.56 million units sold worldwide, it is Nintendo's lowest-selling home console
prompt: A console maker's motion-control console sold extremely well, but its sales are now falling and casual players are moving to phones and tablets. Proposal (2012): launch a follow-up console whose controller has a built-in 6-inch touchscreen, sold under the previous console's brand name with a short suffix, priced at $299 to $349, with HD graphics roughly matching rival consoles released six years earlier. Risks raised: buyers may think it is an accessory for the old console; third-party publishers are lukewarm; rivals will release new consoles within a year; the launch game line-up is thin.

evidence_quote: In response to its poor reception, Facebook indicated in late-May 2013 that it was planning on making improvements to Home in response to consumer feedback.
prompt: A large social network wants more of people's time and attention on smartphones without building its own phone operating system. Proposal (2013): release a replacement home screen and lock screen for an open mobile operating system that puts friends' posts and chat front and center, plus a partner phone that ships with it preinstalled. Risks raised: users may not want the social network to take over their phone's home screen; it works on only a handful of phone models; it pushes the user's other apps out of view; privacy critics are wary of always-on social software.

evidence_quote: In late 2017, Snapchat wrote off $40m worth of unsold Spectacles inventory and unused parts.
prompt: A photo-messaging app company wants a hardware product. Proposal (2016): sell $130 sunglasses with a built-in camera that records 10-second circular videos to the app, first through pop-up vending machines, then scale up manufacturing for wide retail sale. Risks raised: users must pair the glasses with their phone to see the videos; the company has never made hardware; novelty-driven demand may fade; camera glasses raise privacy concerns.

evidence_quote: The Diem Association (originally the Libra Association) shut down in January 2022 and sold the project to Silvergate Bank.
prompt: A social-media company with over two billion users wants to offer payments. Proposal (2019): launch a global digital currency backed by a basket of bank deposits and government securities, governed by an association of large partner companies and usable inside its messaging apps. Risks raised: regulators in the US and Europe may see it as a threat to monetary sovereignty; the company is under scrutiny over privacy scandals and antitrust; partners may withdraw; money-laundering rules differ by country.

evidence_quote: Google announced in September 2022 that it would be shutting down Stadia; the service went offline permanently on January 18, 2023.
prompt: A large internet company with global data centers has no game business. Proposal (2019): launch a cloud gaming service that streams console-quality games to TVs, browsers and phones with no console needed, charging a monthly subscription for 4K play plus full price for each game, and set up its own game studios. Risks raised: streaming quality depends on users' internet connections and adds input lag; players must buy their games again at full price; the company has a reputation for ending products; publishers bring few exclusive games.
